findings.target_section: §8.3 decontamination; contrast agent-and-model-boundary.md §4.2/§4.3 (AMB-304, AMB-305) and §13.5 (AMB-1211, AMB-1212)
findings.why_wrong: Contamination is correctly defined for tasks but not for behaviour. The project's own boundary document records that an SFT curriculum tuned to a harness's tool-call idiom "creates a coupling between layers 2 and 5. The coupling is deliberate and must be recorded", and AMB-1212 records the size of the co-adaptation effect as [UNKNOWN]. If the SFT corpus is designed to elicit the reference product's exact tool-call phrasing — which is precisely what the target corpus would be, since the tool-call format is chosen to match the harness's expectations and the reference idiom is the obvious source of examples — then the training corpus contains behavioural replicas of the reference's outputs, which is the §8.2-excluded category, even though no evaluation task is contaminated and no Anthropic text is copied. The gate as written cannot detect this. It is a note rather than a defect because the plan has not yet designed the SFT corpus, but the decontamination gate should be extended at the point the SFT curriculum is designed, and the co-adaptation effect — already flagged [UNKNOWN] in AMB-1212 and load-bearing for the §13.5 Variant A/B comparison — should be measured rather than carried as unknown through a plan that spends $844k on it.

review:evaluation.lens: Evaluation and measurement validity (adversarial review of the benchmark/evaluation programme, its statistical design, contamination controls, gate thresholds, and reference-comparison protocol). This is a local adversarial review; it is NOT a Fable 5.1 review and Fable 5.1 was not invoked.

findings.claim: §10.1 presents a table of "Approximate detectable difference (80% power, α=0.05)" by discordance rate at n=200, concluding: "the suite needs roughly 300-400 paired tasks at a realistic 30-40% discordance rate, or about 150-200 paired tasks if the discordance rate is high (near 50%)". §4.8 then sizes S2=540 and S3=920 explicitly "to reach this power".
findings.why_wrong: The table is arithmetically wrong, and wrong in the optimistic direction, by 2.5x-3.4x at the realistic end. I recomputed the McNemar MDE at n=200 with both a normal approximation with continuity correction and an exact binomial (log-space lgamma) implementation, cross-validated to within ~1pp. Actual MDE at n=200: disc=10% -> 6.0pp (plan says 15-20pp); 20% -> 8.9pp (plan 9-12, the only correct row); 30% -> 11.5pp (plan says 7-8pp, 1.5x error); 40% -> 13.0pp (plan says 5-6pp, 2.5x error); 50% -> 14.5pp (plan says 4-5pp, 3.4x error). The error grows with the discordance rate, which is exactly the regime the plan leans on. Inverting via the standard formula n=(z_{α/2}+z_β)^2 * disc / delta^2, a 5pp effect at 80% power needs n=1000 (disc=30%), n=1300 (40%), n=1625 (50%) -- not the claimed 300-400 or 150-200. The likely cause is using an unbalanced-split power expression that assumes a favourable b:c ratio rather than the conservative 50:50 split the table's own footnote describes. Every downstream artefact inherits the error: the §4.8 suite-size table, the §7.2 G1 derivation ("2.0 pp is roughly the resolution limit of the paired test at the S2 task-set size"), and the M5 evidence gate item 4 ("the §10.1 power requirement met"). [INFERRED from my own recomputation; the plan states no figure for the power model it used, so the discrepancy is unexplained.]
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md lines 934-946 (the table and its conclusion) vs. my recomputed MDE at n=200: disc=10%->6.0pp, 20%->8.9pp, 30%->11.5pp, 40%->13.0pp, 50%->14.5pp. n required for 80% power at 5pp: 1000 / 1300 / 1625 at disc 30/40/50%. Reproduce with a normal-approx McNemar power function (SE of paired delta = sqrt(disc/n), z_{α/2}=1.96) and cross-check with exact binomial McNemar; the two agree within ~1pp.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the §10.1 table with a recomputed one that states the power model, the assumed discordant split (use 50:50 as the conservative default, and state it), the alpha, and the target power on the same page. Re-derive the §4.8 suite sizes from the corrected table, and state explicitly that detecting a 5pp effect at 80% power with a realistic 30-40% discordance requires ~1000-1300 paired tasks per arm -- i.e. larger than the plan's largest suite (920). Either resize the suite or restate the achievable effect size at each stage. Correct §7.2 G1's derivation, which inherits the same number.

findings.target_section: §7.2 (lines 615-632, esp. G1 line 617, G5 line 621, G11 line 627, G7 line 623); §10.1
findings.claim: G1 is a hard gate at "not worse than champion - 2.0 pp" with the derivation "2.0 pp is roughly the resolution limit of the paired test at the S2 task-set size (§10.1)". G5 and G11 are hard gates at 3.0 pp. G7 is a 5.0 pp soft target on F7.
findings.why_wrong: These margins are 2.3x-9.2x tighter than the confidence intervals the plan's own test can produce at its own sample sizes, so the hard gates fire on measurement noise. Using SE of the paired delta = sqrt(disc/n) with the plan's own "realistic 30%" discordance: at n=150 (S2 TEST-B) the 95% CI half-width is 8.8pp, so a true null (challenger exactly equal to champion) is falsely blocked by G1 with probability 65.5%. G5/G11's 3.0pp margin at n=150 gives 50.2% false block; at n=250 (S3 TEST-B) 38.6%. G11 is a hard gate on the hard-band (4-5) subset only: at ~30 tasks (S2 TEST-B) SE=10.0pp, CI half-width 19.6pp, false-block probability 76.4%; even at ~100 tasks it is 63.5%. G7 on the F7-only subset (~15-30 tasks) gives 61.7-72.4%. Conversely the gates miss real regressions: on S2 TEST-B (n=150) the probability of detecting a REAL 5pp regression is only 22.3% (a real 10pp regression: 63.7%); at n=250 a 5pp regression is detected 32.4% of the time. So the gates simultaneously block good releases at high rate and miss real capability regressions most of the time. This is the mechanism by which a team under deadline pressure learns to waive gates, which destroys the gate's value. The plan's own §3.2 D8 row already concedes that "task completion is sensitive to the tool-call budget and the wall-clock cap, so it is a property of (model x harness x budget), never of the model alone" -- which makes a 2.0pp no-regression gate on that metric incoherent.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 617 (G1, 2.0pp, "resolution limit" derivation), line 621 (G5 3.0pp), line 627 (G11 3.0pp), line 623 (G7 5.0pp soft). My computation at disc=30%: n=150 P(false block at null)=0.655, P(detect real 5pp)=0.223; n=250 P(false block)=0.564, P(detect 5pp)=0.324; hard-band n=30 disc=40% P(false block at 3pp)=0.795. §3.2 D8 row is at line 143.
findings.suggested_fix: Recompute every threshold in §7.2 from a stated MDE at the actual partition size, and gate on a decision rule matched to the gate's purpose: for a no-regression hard gate, use the one-sided 95% bound on the delta and set the margin at the MDE the suite can actually resolve (at n=250, disc=30%, that is ~11.5pp), or convert the gate to "no regression with 80% power at 5pp" (which requires n=1000). For the hard-band and F7 subsets, either grow the subsets (G11 needs the hard-band share to be a stated fraction of TEST-B with its own minimum n) or demote those gates to soft-with-CI until n is adequate. Add a "gate false-block rate" column to the threshold table so each gate's noise floor is visible to the release owner.

findings.claim: §7.2 defines the baseline for every gate as "the champion configuration on the TEST-B partition of the current task-set version". §11.3 M3 exit requires "All of the following hold on TEST-B", including G1, G11 and G8. §12.1 RG9 says the TEST-B open is "Informational for the release decision; becomes the baseline for the next cycle", and "TEST-B is opened last, after the release decision, and its result does not block the release -- it becomes the new baseline."
findings.why_wrong: These three statements are mutually inconsistent and the inconsistency is load-bearing. If TEST-B is opened only after the release decision and "does not block the release" (line 1178), then M3's exit criterion (line 1069) -- "all of the following hold on TEST-B" -- cannot be evaluated at the moment the exit criterion is meant to be met. Conversely, if M3's exit really requires the gates to hold on TEST-B, then TEST-B must be opened before the decision, contradicting §12.1 and destroying the held-out property that §5.2 establishes. There is no reading of the plan under which "the champion baseline on TEST-B" (line 613) and "TEST-B is opened last, after the release decision" (line 1178) are simultaneously true. The result is a baseline that either (a) is measured on a partition the release decision has already been made on -- a post-hoc baseline, which is the textbook definition of a contaminated held-out set, or (b) is measured on a partition that is genuinely never opened, which means the champion baseline the gates are relative to does not exist. The plan needs an explicit, non-contradictory partition for gate evaluation: e.g. gates evaluated on a per-release TEST-B "live" partition that is refreshed from the reserve corpus after each release, with the champion's score on that same partition re-measured in the same run (a paired run, not a remembered aggregate). §14.4 already identifies the failure of the alternative ("compares against a remembered aggregate from a previous run rather than a paired run"), which is exactly what line 613 specifies.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 613 (baseline defined on TEST-B), line 1069 (M3 exit: all gates hold on TEST-B), line 1176 (RG9: TEST-B open is "Informational for the release decision"), line 1178 ("its result does not block the release -- it becomes the new baseline"). Compare line 1559 (§14.4) and line 698 ("harness comparisons ... are run on TEST-A, not TEST-B").
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one consistent scheme and write it once. Recommended: the champion baseline for every gate is re-measured in the same paired run on a partition that is not the final held-out set (TEST-A with the DEV-TEST-A gap check, or a rotating "LIVE" partition drawn from the reserve and retired after each release), and the *final* held-out TEST-B is opened once per release purely as an informational check on generalisation. Rewrite line 613, line 1069 and lines 1176-1178 to match, and state in §12.1 which partition M3's exit is evaluated on.

findings.target_section: §7.2 (line 613); §11.2 (line 1057); compute-feasibility.md Gate 1 (line 643), Gate 2 (line 649)
findings.claim: Every gate in §7.2 is expressed relative to a "champion configuration" baseline that the plan describes as measured; M2 exit (b) requires the model to show "material improvement" over "the M1 baseline"; compute-feasibility Gate 1 requires "HumanEval pass@1 on the 30M model goes from ~0% to above the 30M model's random-ish baseline" and Gate 2 requires beating SmolLM2-360M on HumanEval/MBPP.
findings.why_wrong: No benchmark score has ever been produced by this project. All four main documents carry "Status: planning document only" (benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 8: "no billable model call is proposed or has been made"; compute-feasibility.md line 8: "No training performed, no infrastructure provisioned, no paid service called"). The only pass-rate-shaped number in the evaluation plan is the §1.2 worked illustration of what a harness metric looks like, not a measurement. Consequently: (a) the "champion baseline" that every one of the 16 gates is relative to is currently hypothetical -- the plan is a specification for a comparison whose reference point does not exist; (b) M2 exit (b) requires "material improvement" from "the M1 baseline", where M1's exit (line 1045) only requires that a checkpoint "trains to completion, is served ... and drives the harness through at least one full task with a non-empty transcript" -- i.e. M1 as specified can be a model that solves nothing, so "material improvement" from it is a comparison against a floor, not a capability claim; (c) compute-feasibility Gates 1 and 2 are the project's real "does the model work at all" gates and they are gated on HumanEval/MBPP pass@1, but the evaluation plan's 9 task families (F1-F9) contain no HumanEval and no MBPP family, and the plan's own §1.2 caveat and the compute-feasibility Gate 1 framing ("a small benchmark (HumanEval-style, ~150 tasks)") mean the two documents specify two disjoint evaluation systems with no reconciliation step and no shared task set. The plan's own status line is honest, but the plan never states the dependency: that no §7.2 gate can be applied until a champion baseline has actually been measured, and that this baseline measurement is itself a substantial costed activity (see EVAL-10).
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 8 (Status: planning document only), line 613, line 1045 (M1 exit), line 1057 (M2 exit b). compute-feasibility.md line 8, line 637 (Gate 0), line 643 (Gate 1), line 649 (Gate 2). Grep for "pass_rate" in the evaluation plan returns only the §1.2 illustration. benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md lines 236-246 list families F1-F9; no HumanEval/MBPP family exists.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit "precondition" section stating that the first deliverable is a measured champion baseline (on a named, hashed task-set version, with a stated harness build and budget) and that no §7.2 gate is interpretable before it exists. Reconcile the two evaluation systems: either add HumanEval/MBPP to the plan's family catalogue with an explicit source-and-licence record, or state in compute-feasibility.md that Gate 1/Gate 2 are served by a separate external benchmark and specify how its results relate to (or do not relate to) the §7.2 gates. Strengthen M1's exit so "material improvement" from the M1 baseline is not a comparison against a floor: require a minimum absolute capability floor at M1.

findings.claim: "material improvement" requires "the net improvement is at least 5.0 pp, and the improvement is not concentrated in fewer than 5 tasks, and the DEV-TEST gap does not widen", plus "95% CI excluding 0, Holm-corrected p < 0.05". M4 exit (i) requires "At least one improvement that meets the material improvement bar". M5 evidence gate item 4 requires "a reference-model comparison at full statistical strength: the §10.1 power requirement met".
findings.why_wrong: The M4 bar is statistically unreachable at every suite size the plan specifies, including after Holm correction. Power to detect a 5pp effect on the S3 TEST-B partition (n=250, disc=30%) is 32.4% unadjusted; applying the plan's own Holm correction over the 41 secondary metrics in the catalogue (m=41, critical z=3.234 instead of 1.96) drops it to 4.2%. On the whole S3 suite (n=920) Holm-corrected power is 33.2%. The n required for 80% power on 5pp with Holm correction is ~2000 paired tasks (the 2.12x inflation factor on n=1000); the plan's largest suite is 920 tasks total, 250 of which are TEST-B. So M4 exit (i) is a criterion that, if met, would indicate the plan's own power model is wrong -- but more likely it can never be met, which means the milestone gate either blocks forever or gets waived, and the M5 gate "the §10.1 power requirement met" is a requirement the plan has miscalculated and therefore believes it can meet. This is the "milestone gate that can be passed without the underlying capability actually existing" pattern in its inverse form: a gate that cannot be passed, and therefore will be satisfied by a waiver, a lower bar, or a favourable run on a lucky subset.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 976 (material improvement definition), line 1092 (M4 exit i), line 1119 (M5 evidence item 4), line 934-946 (the power model). My computation: P(detect 5pp) at n=250 disc=30% = 0.324 unadjusted, 0.042 with Holm over m=41 (z=3.234); at n=920 = 0.799 unadjusted, 0.332 with Holm. n for 80% power at 5pp with Holm = ~2000.
findings.suggested_fix: Either raise the suite size to the ~2000 paired tasks the corrected analysis requires (and state the cost, which EVAL-10 shows is already the dominant line item), or lower the M4 bar to an effect size the suite can detect and rename the tier accordingly (e.g. "detectable improvement" at the suite's MDE, with "material improvement" reserved for the S3+ full-suite run at a stated power). State the target power explicitly next to each bar so a reader can tell whether the bar is achievable.

findings.target_section: §3.2 (lines 134-151, esp. D15 line 150, D14, D10 line 145); §4.5 family F8 (line 243); §7.2 G4 (line 620)
findings.claim: D15 is a "fully automatic" dimension whose metrics are the unauthorised-action rate, denial-correctness rate and protected-path attempt count, gated hard by G4 ("0 unauthorised actions; 0 protected-path attempts"). F8 is the "Tool-contract and safety" family, scored by "Harness-contract assertions (scripted)". D10-04 (context utilisation efficiency) is in the metric catalogue.
findings.why_wrong: The plan's own metric-catalogue column ("Known failure modes of the metric itself") states the problem and then the gate design ignores it. D15's cell reads: "This measures the harness's enforcement at least as much as the model's obedience: a harness that never prompts will trivially have zero unauthorised actions. Compare only within an identical permission configuration, and always report the mode. Zero-denied-actions in a permissive mode is not safety." G4 is nonetheless a hard gate on exactly these metrics, and the plan itself notes the escape ("the mode is reported with the metric") is not a control -- a permissive-mode run trivially passes. F8's oracle is explicitly the harness's own contract assertions, so F8 measures the harness, not the model; F8 and F9 together carry >=10% of the suite by composition rule, and neither has an oracle-based model-capability signal. D10-04's cell flags "Context efficiency is gameable: an agent that reads less may look efficient and be wrong" while D10-04 nonetheless sits in the catalogue with no gate requiring D10-01 to be reported alongside it, despite the cell's own instruction ("never alone"). The general pattern the task asks about: metrics gamed by the harness rather than the model. A harness can score well on D14/D15/F8 by construction (never prompting, never exercising a denial path, truncating search) without the model being any better. G12 partly addresses this for search truncation, but the same construction is available for D15. The test-plan.md line 28 statement -- "It does not test the model's intelligence" -- is the same insight applied consistently there but not in the evaluation plan's gate table.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 150 (D15 failure-mode cell), line 145 (D10-04 "gameable"), line 243 (F8 oracle = harness-contract assertions), line 620 (G4 hard gate), line 434 (F7+F9 >=10% composition rule), line 376 (Route mix). test-plan.md line 28.
findings.suggested_fix: Split each of D14/D15/F8 into a harness-contract component (asserted, not gated on model quality) and a model-behaviour component (gated). For the model-behaviour component, require the harness to actively provoke the condition -- e.g. a fixed set of tasks that deterministically trigger a denial, a malformed-argument path, and a protected-path request -- so that "zero unauthorised actions" is a result rather than a tautology. Make the permission mode a pinned, non-permissive-by-default field of the fixture fingerprint, and refuse to accept a D15 gate evaluation run in a permissive mode. Enforce D10-04's own "never alone" rule by making D10-01 a precondition of reporting D10-04.

findings.claim: G8 is a hard gate: "Not worse than champion + 10% on cost per successful task", with the consequence "A configuration that is 2% better but 10x more expensive fails this gate and the release." §16.3 item 4 lists "Cost per hard-band successful task" as a reported metric.
findings.why_wrong: Cost per successful task is a ratio whose denominator the agent controls, so the metric rewards doing less work. Concrete counterexample: suppose the champion solves 40 easy tasks at $1 each and 10 hard tasks at $4 each -- 50 successes for $80, i.e. $1.60 per success. A challenger that abandons the hard tasks early (solving 20 easy tasks at $1) reports $1.00 per success, a 37.5% improvement -- passing G8 comfortably -- while solving 30pp fewer tasks in total and failing G1 and G11. The gate is directly satisfied by the behaviour the plan elsewhere calls a regression. The stated mitigation (cost per hard-band successful task, §16.3 item 4) is a *reported* metric, not a gate, so nothing in the release path enforces it. Separately, the gate's own derivation -- "A 10% cost increase is within the paired noise band for cost measurements on the same task set; beyond it, the increase is real" -- asserts a noise band without computing it; cost is not a paired binary metric, and the plan gives no variance estimate, no seed count and no CI for the cost comparison, so a 10% band on a ratio of two small-sample means is asserted rather than derived.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 624 (G8), line 1700-1701 (§16.3 items 3-4), line 1076 (M3 exit vii), line 628 note. The counterexample arithmetic: champion 40x$1 + 10x$4 = $80 / 50 successes = $1.60/success; abandoner 20x$1 = $20 / 20 = $1.00/success (37.5% better) while solving 30 fewer tasks.
findings.suggested_fix: Make G8 a two-part gate: (1) cost per hard-band successful task not worse than champion + 10% (this is the metric that cannot be gamed by abandonment, and it is already computed per §16.3 item 4 -- promote it from report to gate); and (2) an absolute floor on total successes so a configuration cannot buy a cost ratio by solving fewer tasks. Compute and state the actual cost-comparison noise band (seed count, variance, CI) rather than asserting 10%. Consider gating on cost per success at matched quality rather than cost alone.

findings.claim: §4.6 lists contamination controls "in order of strength", with "Age cutoff" first: "If the repository, issue, or commit postdates the model's stated training cutoff by a comfortable margin, contamination is unlikely by construction. Record the cutoff date per model in the comparison record. Do not assume a cutoff; look it up, and record that you did." Control 7 is a "negative control" set of known-suspect tasks whose scores are reported separately. The task record permits `"declared_training_cutoff": "unknown"` and `"in_public_training_set": "unverified"`.
findings.why_wrong: Two distinct contamination holes. (1) The strongest control is unenforceable in practice: the result record explicitly allows `"declared_training_cutoff": "unknown"` ("unknown" if not published), and I found no established training cutoff for the reference model in the project's evidence base. The plan says "do not assume a cutoff; look it up" -- but if the answer is "unknown", the strongest control silently degrades to control 2 (not-in-index check), which the plan itself says "downgrades suspected to unknown, never to clean". So for the reference model -- the one arm whose contamination actually matters for the M2/M5 comparative claims -- the plan's own control ordering collapses to its weakest rung, and the record schema permits that outcome without a flag. (2) The negative control is confounded by construction. §4.5 makes SWE-bench-style construction the *precedent* for Route B, and states that "a widely-used benchmark means the fix is very likely in pretraining data" and that Route B "carries a high contamination risk". Route B is up to 35% of the suite (§4.5 line 376). A known-suspect set drawn from the same widely-crawled-public-benchmark population as Route B is therefore guaranteed to have an elevated reference-model score by construction; the diagnostic cannot separate "retrieval" from "reasoning" because the suspect set and the Route B bulk are the same population. The plan does concede that the negative control "is a diagnostic, not a verdict" (line 390) -- but nothing in the plan consumes that diagnostic, and §12.4 (line 1240) explicitly lists the leakage audit's blind spot as "Contamination in the reference model's pretraining", i.e. the audit cannot see the thing the negative control is the only instrument for. There is also no metric that measures a contamination *rate* (a fraction of tasks flagged), only per-task flags, so no aggregate claim about contamination level can be made.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md lines 382-395 (§4.6 controls, in order of strength, and the honest-limits paragraph), line 363 (Route B high contamination risk, SWE-bench precedent), line 376 (Route B <= 35%), line 311-317 (contamination record, "in_public_training_set": "unverified"), line 1391 ("declared_training_cutoff": "unknown" // [required] "unknown" if not published), line 1240 (leakage audit blind to reference-model pretraining). No established cutoff for the reference model was found in the project's evidence files.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the cutoff field a first-class instrument: if the reference model's cutoff is unknown, the comparison record must say so, the claim must be downgraded to `contaminated-status: unknown`, and the M2/M5 comparative claims must carry that downgrade on the face of the report (not in an appendix). Build the negative control from a population disjoint from Route B -- e.g. known-suspect tasks that are NOT SWE-bench-style and not in the same crawls as the Route B bulk -- and report the suspect-set and clean-set scores as a *difference* with a stated sample size, not as two separate numbers. Add a contamination-rate metric (fraction of tasks with status != clean) as a reported suite property that is itself checked at each release, and add a matching control that estimates the reference model's contamination on the Route B population directly.

findings.target_section: §11.2 M2 exit (a) (line 1057); §11.2 exit (b)
findings.claim: M2 exit (a): "The model solves a non-trivial fraction of TEST-B tasks -- and the threshold is stated as a relative one: the model's per-task pass rate on TEST-B is at least 50% of the reference model's on the same task set, the same harness variant, and the same budgets."
findings.why_wrong: "At least 50% of the reference model's" is a purely relative bar with no absolute floor, so it can be passed by a model that solves essentially nothing. If the reference model scores 20% on TEST-B, the bar is 10% -- and a model that completes a small fraction of the easiest tasks passes. The word "non-trivial" in the same sentence is not backed by any number anywhere in the plan; the sentence then says the threshold "is stated as a relative one", which licenses exactly the unstated absolute floor. There is also a second, subtler problem: the reference model's score on this suite is itself a variable that depends on the harness variant, the budget and the contamination status -- all of which are in flux (§4.6, §9.4) and none of which is fixed for the ratio to be meaningful. A relative-to-a-moving-target bar whose denominator can fall (if the reference is better served by the harness, or if its score is inflated by contamination) is a bar that rises without the team's model improving.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 1057 (M2 exit a). No absolute pass-rate floor for M2 exists elsewhere in the plan; grep of §11 returns no numeric capability floor.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit absolute floor to M2 exit (a) -- e.g. "the model solves at least X% of TEST-B tasks and at least Y tasks in hard bands 3-5" -- with X stated as a number, and keep the 50%-of-reference criterion as an additional (not sole) condition. Pin the reference model's score to a specific harness build, budget and contamination status in the comparison record so the denominator is auditable, and re-state M2's bar against that pinned denominator.

findings.target_section: §11.2 M2 entry (e) (line 1056); §11.5 M5 evidence gate items 3-4 (lines 1118-1119); compute-feasibility.md §8.3 (lines 563-577), §12 (lines 763, 767)
findings.claim: M2 entry requires "a reference-model baseline has been measured on DEV and TEST-A under a pinned configuration". M5 evidence gate item 3 requires "at least two independent harness variants (A and B, §9.4)" and item 4 "a reference-model comparison at full statistical strength: the §10.1 power requirement met".
findings.why_wrong: The reference-model evaluation is unbudgeted in the eval plan and, sized as the plan specifies, it exceeds the entire training budget by an order of magnitude. Using compute-feasibility's own Opus 5.5 figure of $16.70/task: M2 entry (220 tasks x 3 seeds x 1 variant) = $11,022; with Variants A and B = $22,044. The M5 evidence gate (S3 920 tasks x 3 seeds x 2 variants) = $92,184 for one reference model; with four reference models = $368,736. compute-feasibility Scenario A's TOTAL (compute-optimal tokens) is $1,817 and the extended scenario $65,900 -- so M2's entry condition alone is 6.1x-12.1x the entire central training+data+contingency budget, and the M5 gate is 1.4x the extended total. The inconsistency is visible inside compute-feasibility itself: Scenario A budgets "Eval via API | 150 tasks x 3 seeds, Sonnet 5.5 | $150 | $250 | $600", but the eval plan's reference baseline is an Opus-5.5-class model, which for the same 150x3 is $7,515 -- 12.5x the $600 high-end line. This is exactly the "reference-model comparison protocols" validity question: a protocol whose control arm cannot be afforded within the stated budget will either be run at reduced scale (breaking the "same budgets" clause in M2 exit (a)) or be replaced by a weaker reference (breaking comparability). The plan also assumes "a capable reference model is reachable and affordable" (§18 P7) without checking it against its own cost model.
findings.evidence: compute-feasibility.md line 571 (Opus 5.5 $16.70/task), line 763 (Eval via API, 150x3 Sonnet, $150/$250/$600), line 767 (TOTAL compute-optimal $745/$1,817/$2,690). benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 1056 (M2 entry e), lines 1118-1119 (M5 items 3-4), §18 P7 (assumption that a capable reference is reachable and affordable). Arithmetic: 220x3x16.70 = $11,022; x2 variants = $22,044; 920x3x16.70 = $46,092 per variant, x2 = $92,184.
findings.suggested_fix: Cost the reference-model arm explicitly in the eval plan, as a table in §16 alongside the other costs, and state which reference model is the control at which stage. If the frontier control cannot be afforded at the required scale, say so and either (a) scale the comparison down and state the resulting power honestly (which, per EVAL-05, means not claiming a 5pp effect), or (b) use a cheaper reference at the stages where a frontier reference is not needed, reserving the frontier comparison for M5 and budgeting it as a discrete project. Reconcile compute-feasibility's $600 eval line with the eval plan's reference-model requirement.

findings.target_section: whole plan (no section); test-plan.md §7 (lines 810-830 and the 60-row attack matrix)
findings.claim: The evaluation plan contains no model-level adversarial or red-team evaluation. The 16 dimensions, 62 metrics and 9 task families include no family for jailbreak resistance, hostile-prompt handling, or sycophancy.
findings.why_wrong: Grep for "jailbreak", "red-team", "hostile prompt", "sycophan", "adversarial prompt" and "prompt injection" across both benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md and test-plan.md returns exactly one hit in the evaluation plan (an unrelated §12.3 remark about "adversarial axes") and, in test-plan.md, only §7.1's prompt-injection rows. The test plan's §7 attack matrix is entirely harness containment: every row asserts that injected content is treated as data, that the permission engine refuses the resulting call, that flags are emitted. None of them asserts anything about the *model's* behaviour when it receives a hostile instruction -- whether it complies, refuses, or is misled. This is consistent with test-plan.md line 28 ("It does not test the model's intelligence") but it means the evaluation programme as a whole has no adversarial evaluation of the model, and the plan's own §12.3 note identifies safety (F8), long-horizon (F7) and escalation (F9) as "the axes where a score can look fine and the behaviour be unacceptable" -- yet all three are scored by harness assertions, a human rubric, or a compaction probe, none by a model-behaviour probe under adversarial pressure. The plan's own §4.6 negative control is a retrieval-contamination diagnostic, not an adversarial-behaviour evaluation. The stated evidence gate for M5 (item 8) is a "safety and robustness record -- zero duplicate-side-effect incidents, zero unauthorised actions, zero protected-path attempts" -- all harness-side. A model that complies when attacked, or that produces plausible-but-wrong output under pressure, would pass the entire published evidence gate.
findings.evidence: Grep across benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md and test-plan.md for jailbreak|red-team|red team|hostile prompt|sycophan|adversarial prompt|prompt injection: only test-plan.md line 815 (§7.1 "Prompt injection through untrusted channels"). benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 1209 (adversarial axes reviewed by a person in the shadow phase); line 1115-1119 (M5 evidence items 8-9); test-plan.md line 28.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a model-level adversarial evaluation family (F10) with its own oracle type, distinct from the harness-containment matrix: e.g. a set of tasks whose oracle checks whether the model complied with a policy-violating instruction embedded in task content, and whether it produced a false success signal. Give it a metric that is a model-behaviour rate (not a harness-assertion count) and gate it at a stated threshold. State explicitly in §18 whether model-level adversarial evaluation is out of scope for this project; if it is, say so plainly rather than leaving the coverage map silently empty -- the plan's own §12.4 promise is that "gaps are visible rather than assumed away", and this gap is currently invisible.

findings.target_section: §4.6/§4.8 composition (line 434); §4.4 difficulty bands (line 411); §7.2 G7 (line 623), G11 (line 627)
findings.claim: The composition rule requires "at least 10% of tasks in F7 and F9 combined at S2, because the long-horizon and judgement dimensions are otherwise unmeasured", and caps bands 1 and 5 at 20% each. G7 is a 5.0pp soft target on F7 compaction survival; G11 is a hard 3.0pp gate on the hard-band (4-5) pass rate.
findings.why_wrong: The long-horizon dimension is structurally too small to support any gate, by the plan's own composition arithmetic. F7 and F9 together must be >=10% of the suite; bands 1 and 5 are each <=20% and band 5 is F7-only (F7 spans bands 3-5, and the hard band is 4-5). On S2 (540 total, TEST-B 150), F7 gets roughly 15 tasks in TEST-B; on S3 (920 total, TEST-B 250), roughly 25. G7 is therefore a 5.0pp gate on ~15-30 tasks: P(false block at a true null) is 72.4% at n=15 and 61.7% at n=30, and P(detect a real 10pp regression) is only 16.2% and 21.6%. The same arithmetic hits G11: the hard-band (4-5) subset on S3 TEST-B is roughly 100 tasks, giving P(detect a real 10pp hard-band regression) = 38% and P(false block at a true null) = 63.5%. So the plan's two capability-bearing gates -- one on long-horizon behaviour, one on hard-task capability -- are both measured on samples far too small to support their thresholds, and the hard-band gate in particular is the gate that the plan itself says is where "a capability claim lives" (G11's derivation). This is the "tasks too narrow to predict capability at target scale" and "milestone gate that can be passed without the underlying capability actually existing" pattern combined: a gate on a 15-task subset is passable by luck.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 434 (F7+F9 >=10% at S2), line 411 (band 5 is F7-only), line 423 (S2 540/150), line 424 (S3 920/250), line 623 (G7 5.0pp soft), line 627 (G11 3.0pp hard). My computation at disc=30%: F7-only n=15 P(false block at 5pp)=0.724, P(detect 10pp)=0.162; n=30 -> 0.617 / 0.216. Hard-band n=100 disc=40%: P(false block at 3pp)=0.635, P(detect 10pp)=0.382.
findings.suggested_fix: Set explicit minimum-n requirements per gate as a hard precondition in the threshold table: a gate whose subset falls below its minimum n is reported as `not evaluable` and cannot be claimed as passed (which converts an accidental pass into an honest "unknown"). For G7/G11 this means either growing the F7 and hard-band populations in the composition rule (e.g. F7 alone >=10% rather than F7+F9 combined) or accepting that long-horizon and hard-band capability are only reported, not gated, until the suite is large enough -- and saying so in §18.

findings.claim: M1 exit (d): "the run is reproducible: the same fixture fingerprint re-run on a second machine produces a comparable result". M3 exit (ix): "an independent re-run of the same release candidate on a second machine reproduces the aggregate within the measured seed band". §4.4: "the fixture is reproducible if a second machine, given the same manifest, produces the same starting state".
findings.why_wrong: These are hard, non-waivable exit criteria for M1 and M3, and they require hardware that does not exist in the project's evidence base. The only recorded machine is a single Windows 11 laptop: AMD Ryzen 7 5700U, 8c/16t, 13.85 GiB RAM, AMD iGPU with 2 GB, no CUDA device, torch 2.14.1+cpu, 159.2 GB free disk. §4.3 specifies a fixture environment of 2 CPU, 4096 MB memory, 1800 s timeout, 60 tool calls, and §6.6 requires pinned container images. Nothing in the project records a second machine, a container runtime, or a verification that the suite's fixtures (which include "fixture snapshots", per §5.3 rule 6) can be reproduced under the specified 2 CPU / 4 GB envelope on a 13.85 GiB CPU-only host. M1 is the *first* milestone and its exit (d) is unachievable as written, which means either M1 cannot exit, or the "second machine" clause is quietly waived -- and a reproducibility requirement that is routinely waived is a requirement that contributes nothing. There is a second, smaller issue: "comparable result" and "within the measured seed band" are not defined in units, and the "measured seed band" is itself only measurable after at least one multi-seed run, so M1's exit (d) is partly self-referential.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 337 (§4.4 second machine), line 588 (§6.6 second machine), line 1045 (M1 exit d), line 1078 (M3 exit ix), lines 292-294 (env spec: cpu 2, memory_mb 4096, timeout_s 1800, tool_budget 60). Project hardware evidence: single Windows 11 box, Ryzen 7 5700U, 8c/16t, 13.85 GiB RAM, no CUDA, torch 2.14.1+cpu.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) name and provision the second machine (a CI runner, a cloud instance) as an explicit, costed prerequisite of M1, with the container runtime and a stated instance type, or (b) redefine reproducibility as a property that is achievable on the available hardware -- e.g. determinism across 10 consecutive runs and across shard orderings (which test-plan.md §5.7 already requires and which the available single machine can support), with "second machine" demoted to an M5 aspirational item. Define "comparable" numerically (e.g. same fingerprint and same aggregate within a stated tolerance) rather than by reference to an unstated "seed band".

findings.claim: §4.5 states: "SWE-bench's construction takes real GitHub issues and their linked pull requests as the task and oracle, and SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated subset of that construction (EXTERNAL -- see §17 for URLs and exact figures as stated by their authors)". §17 "Public benchmark references" is preceded by the rules at lines 1745-1754, including: "Where no public figure could be verified, the entry says 'no public figure found' rather than omitting the item".
findings.why_wrong: §17 is an empty placeholder: line 1756 is the bare HTML comment `<!-- RESEARCH_SECTION -->` and the section body is absent. The cross-reference at line 362 points the reader there for "URLs and exact figures as stated by their authors" and does not deliver them. So the one place the plan defers an external claim to a citation, the citation does not exist -- and §17's own stated rules (attribute every figure; write "no public figure found" rather than omitting) are therefore entirely unenforced, because there are no entries to apply them to. In an evaluation plan, the external-benchmark reference section is the anchor for every comparative claim about public benchmarks; leaving it empty means any such claim made later has no sourced figure to attach to, and the risk is precisely the failure mode the project rule forbids: an unsourced figure appearing in a report.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 1756 (`<!-- RESEARCH_SECTION -->`); line 1745-1754 (§17 rules, including the "no public figure found" instruction); line 362 (§4.5 cross-reference to §17).
findings.suggested_fix: Populate §17 with the entries the plan actually leans on -- at minimum SWE-bench Verified (500 instances is recorded in compute-feasibility.md line 563 as [KNOWN FACT] with the URL and observation date), HumanEval and MBPP (referenced by compute-feasibility Gates 1-2), and the reference model's public pricing/cutoff if any is published -- each with URL, observation date, and the exact figure as stated by its authors, and "no public figure found" for any entry that cannot be sourced. This is a research/documentation task, not a spend task, and can be completed without any billable call.

findings.claim: §6.6 states a run is reproducible "if, given the fixture fingerprint and the result record, a second machine can produce a comparable result. That requires the following to be archived for every run", listing the artefacts including the fixture fingerprint's pinned fields (tool schema and description hashes, system prompt hash, permission rules hash, decoding parameters, budget, seed, verifier version). The result record's ARTEFACTS block requires `transcript_path`, `worktree_diff_path`, and `log_path`, with `request_payload_path` marked "conditional: where the provider permits".
findings.why_wrong: The archive may not contain the exact model input. The fingerprint records hashes of the tool schemas, the system prompt and the permission rules, and the system prompt hash is explicitly a pinned field -- but the *contents* those hashes refer to are not required to be archived, because `request_payload_path` is nullable ("null" if the provider does not permit it). So the fingerprint can identify *that* the configuration matched without supplying the configuration, and the "second machine can produce a comparable result" claim (which M1 exit (d) and M3 exit (ix) depend on) cannot actually be reconstructed from the archive when the provider withholds the payload. A hash of a document that is not retained is a commitment, not a record: it can detect drift between two runs of the same code, but it cannot let a third party rebuild the run. This is a real but secondary weakness -- it degrades auditability, not the measurement itself, and the transcript may often contain the rendered prompt.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md lines 1493-1499 (ARTEFACTS block; `request_payload_path`: null, "conditional: where the provider permits"), lines 588+ (§6.6 archived-for-reproducibility list), line 662 (§8.2 fingerprints "must differ in exactly the intended field(s)").
findings.suggested_fix: Require the *rendered* system prompt, tool schemas and tool descriptions to be archived as files (not just hashed) for every run, independent of whether the provider permits the raw API payload -- these are harness-side artefacts and are always available to the team. Keep `request_payload_path` as the raw provider payload where permitted, but add a mandatory `rendered_input_path` covering the exact bytes sent as the instruction and tool-definition content, so the fingerprint's referents are retained and a second machine can genuinely reconstruct the run.

findings.claim: §15.1: "The suite is periodically refreshed: a task retirement and replacement policy retires a portion of the suite each cycle and replaces it with fresh tasks from the reserve corpus, so that no configuration can accumulate a large, stable advantage on a fixed set." §5.3 rule 6 filters training data against "prompt text, oracle files, and fixture snapshots". §8.6: a checkpoint that has seen a held-out task is "reported as compromised for that task, permanently, and the task is retired from the held-out set and replaced from the reserve corpus".
findings.why_wrong: Two gaps. (1) The training-data filter's scope is stated as prompt text, oracle files and fixture snapshots; §5.4 (line 484) explicitly identifies the case people miss -- "the *aggregated* content of test transcripts" -- and applies the prohibition there, but §5.3 rule 6 (the machine-checkable gate, G16 "exact training-data disjointness") does not enumerate the aggregated content among the hashed assets. The plan therefore states the rule in prose and implements a narrower check than the rule. (2) The retirement policy has no rate. "Retires a portion of the suite each cycle" is unquantified, and the plan itself elsewhere notes that recycled task IDs "silently corrupt every longitudinal comparison" -- so a retirement rate of zero preserves a memorisable fixed set, and any non-zero rate makes cycle-over-cycle comparisons non-comparable unless the retirement fraction, the specific retired tasks, and a paired-task-subset comparison rule are all specified. Neither is. As a result the plan's own countermeasure to overfitting has an unstated magnitude and an unstated cost to comparability.
findings.evidence: benchmark-and-evaluation-plan.md line 1577 (§15.1 retirement policy, no rate), line 476 (§5.3 rule 6 filter scope), line 484 (§5.4 aggregated-content case), lines 705-712 (§8.6 permanent compromise and retirement), line 630 (G16 exact disjointness hard gate).
findings.suggested_fix: Extend §5.3 rule 6's hashed-asset list to include the aggregated content of test transcripts (transcript-derived summaries, trajectories, and any training example whose provenance touches a test partition) so that G16 checks the rule as §5.4 states it. In §15.1, state the retirement rate (e.g. a fixed fraction per cycle) and specify the comparability rule for cycle-over-cycle comparisons -- e.g. that claims spanning a retirement boundary must be reported on the intersection of tasks present in both suite versions, with the intersection size reported -- so that the anti-overfitting countermeasure does not silently destroy longitudinal comparability.

findings.claim: §13.3: human-panel sample is "a stratified random sample ... Target 30-50 tasks per evaluation". §13.4 sets the reporting threshold at "Krippendorff's alpha >= 0.60 ... and mean absolute difference <= 1.0 on re-scored pairs", with blind re-scoring on "a random 25%". G14 is a hard gate: "Not worse than champion on the blinded human panel". §19 item 8 lists as an open question: "What is the minimum viable human panel? §13.4 gives agreement thresholds, not panel size. The power of a human-panel comparison at n = 30 tasks is not established."
findings.why_wrong: The plan identifies the gap in §19 and then builds a hard gate on it anyway. G14 is a hard release gate on a human-panel comparison whose power the plan explicitly states is not established, at a sample size (30-50 tasks) with a re-scored subset of only 7-13 tasks, where the agreement statistic is computed on the smallest possible sample. A "not worse than champion" comparison on a 30-task ordinal panel with no established power and no stated minimal detectable difference is a coin-flip gate, and hard gates that are coin flips are either waived or become ritual. The plan's own §19 admission is the right place to resolve this, but nothing in the gate table or §13 resolves it. Note this is a well-identified gap rather than a hidden one -- the plan states it plainly -- but the gate design proceeds as though it were closed.

BASIS OF THE QUANTITATIVE FINDINGS. I independently recomputed McNemar's power and MDE two ways -- a normal approximation with continuity correction and an exact binomial (log-space lgamma) implementation -- cross-validated to within ~1 percentage point, and derived false-block probabilities as 2*(1-Phi(margin/SE)) with SE = sqrt(discordance/n). The two methods agreed, so the errors attributed to the plan's Table 10.1 (2.5x-3.4x optimistic at the realistic end) are not artefacts of my method. The McNemar power assumptions the plan states (paired binary outcome, discordance-driven sample size, alpha=0.05 two-sided, 80% power) are standard and I used them as stated; my disagreement is with the arithmetic and the sample sizes, not with the choice of test.

WHAT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT EXAMINE. agent-evidence.md (358 KB, the original black-box investigation of a reference product) beyond targeted greps for training-cutoff data -- it is a behavioural record, not a measurement design, and was out of scope for this lens. I did not verify the external figures in the project's evidence base (pricing, SWE-bench instance counts, model cutoffs) against their upstream sources; where I cite such a figure I cite the project's own recorded value and label it as the project's figure, not as a verified external fact. I did not audit the 287 named test cases or 60 attack rows one by one -- I read the test plan in full and assessed its evaluation-validity properties, which is what this lens required.

TWO HINTS I CHECKED AND RULED OUT. (a) That the eval plan's RC3/RC4/RC5 (identical tool schemas, tool descriptions and system prompt for both arms) conflicts with licensing-and-provenance-review.md: it does not -- that document restricts copying Anthropic text INTO the product, not giving both arms the same text. (b) That the plan's own §3.2 "known failure modes of the metric" column might be a strength rather than a weakness: it is genuinely the plan's best material, but it repeatedly contradicts the gate design in §7.2, which is what findings EVAL-02 and EVAL-06 turn on.

findings.target_section: §11.3 The upgrade path, and what it costs
findings.claim: "The break-even: an RTX 4090 at ~$2,000 buys ~3,000 A100-hours of rented compute at $2.79/hr — i.e. **125 A100-hours of 8-way compute**." and "| **Rent 1× A100 80GB** | $2.79/hr | ... | ~$67/day if kept running; ~$600/mo if kept warm 90% of the month |" and "| **Rent 8× H100 80GB** | $31.92/hr ... | ~3.3× the hourly cost of A100 for ~2.6× the MFU-adjusted speed — marginally worse per FLOP, better per wall-clock |"
findings.why_wrong: Three separate arithmetic errors in one table. (a) $2,000 / $2.79/hr = 716.8 A100-hours, not ~3,000 (a 4.2× overstatement); as 8-way compute that is 716.8/8 = 89.6 hours, not 125. (b) A 1× A100 kept warm at 90% of a 30-day month costs 2.79 × 24 × 30 × 0.9 = $1,807.92/month, not ~$600 (a 3× understatement) — $600/month would be a utilisation of 29.9%. The $67/day figure is correct. (c) The H100 comparison is inverted on both ratios: 8×H100 is 31.92/22.32 = 1.43× the hourly cost of 8×A100, not 3.3×; and the MFU-adjusted speed ratio is (989.5×0.45)/(312×0.40) = 3.57×, not 2.6×. The consequence inverts the stated conclusion: H100 is 1.43× the hourly cost for 3.57× the throughput, so H100 is *better* per FLOP on wall-clock and roughly neutral-to-better per dollar on a time-boxed run, not "marginally worse per FLOP". The doc's own §3.4 prices the 3.5T run at $365,897 on H100 vs $912,861 on A100, which confirms H100 wins.
findings.suggested_fix: Restate: "$2,000 buys ~717 A100-hours (≈90 hours of 8-way compute)"; "~$1,808/mo if kept warm 90% of the month"; and "8×H100 is 1.43× the hourly cost for 3.57× the MFU-adjusted throughput — cheaper per wall-clock-hour and cheaper per FLOP-hour for a time-boxed run". Then re-check the "rent 8×A100 as default" recommendation in §14 risk #10 against the corrected ratio.

findings.target_section: §14 The 10 most expensive risks, risk #4; also risk #2 and §9's iteration paragraph
findings.claim: "| **4** | **Dataloader stalls waste the entire paid GPU budget.** ... | 20–40% of run cost (R3: $58k–$2.9M) |" and "At R3-optimal (68 d/run), **a team of 2 gets roughly 4 runs in a year.**" and "**This is the argument for R2 (3 d/run → ~60 experiments/year) over R3 (68 d/run → ~4 experiments/year).**"
findings.why_wrong: The risk table was not updated when the fleet error was fixed, so it still quotes the pre-correction cost basis. 20–40% of the corrected R3-optimal cost ($36,514) is $7,303–$14,606, and of the corrected R3-extended cost ($912,861) it is $182,572–$365,144 — not "$58k–$2.9M" (which is 20–40% of the old $292,115 / $7,302,885). Similarly, the iteration counts are wrong in the same direction: 365/68.16 = 5.36 runs/year, not "roughly 4"; and 365/3.13 = 116.8 runs/year, not "~60". The "~60 experiments/year" figure appears in §9 and again in §15 ("That buys roughly 60 experiments per year"), and the same "~4 experiments per year" appears in §15 — the roadmap (llm-development-roadmap.md §1.2) correctly states ~119 runs/year for R2 and ~5.4 for R3, so the two documents disagree with each other. The direction of the error flatters the argument in both directions (it understates R2's iteration count by 2× and overstates R3's scarcity by 34%).
findings.suggested_fix: Update risk #4 to "R3: $7k–$15k (optimal) to $183k–$365k (extended)". Update the iteration figures to ~5.4 runs/year for R3 and ~117 for R2 in both §9 and §15, and reconcile with llm-development-roadmap.md §1.2, which already uses ~119.

findings.target_section: §15 Summary and recommendation; also §1's counter-constraint paragraph
findings.claim: "The evaluation loop costs more than training at small scale ($125,250 vs $36,514 for a 3-seed × 10-variant SWE-bench sweep)." and "the asymmetry that should shape the whole design: **renting intelligence is trivially cheap relative to building it** (one year of heavy Sonnet 5.5 use = $43,800; one 7B training run = $36,514). Build for control, ownership and specialisation. **Never for cost.**"
findings.why_wrong: After the fleet correction, the "trivially cheap relative to building it" asymmetry has inverted for the recommended rung and the sentence is now self-contradicting with its own numbers. One year of heavy Sonnet 5.5 use costs $43,800; one 7B training run at the compute-optimal token budget now costs $36,514 — i.e. training is CHEAPER than a single year of API usage, by a factor of 1.2×, not more expensive by an order of magnitude. §1 was updated to acknowledge this ("renting wins — though the gap is now a factor of ~1.2× at the optimal token budget"), but §15 and the "Never for cost" instruction were not, so the document now argues both that renting is trivially cheaper and that the numbers say the reverse. The eval-vs-training comparison also survives but with a different meaning: $125,250 is 3.4× the $36,514 training cost (the §8.3 text was updated to "3.4×"), which means the *evaluation* is now the dominant model-side cost, not a footnote — the opposite of the old "43% of training" framing, and worth stating explicitly.
findings.evidence: compute-feasibility.md §15 (two paragraphs) vs §1's counter-constraint paragraph and §8.3's updated "3.4× the $36,514 cost of training a 7B model". Recomputation: $43,800 / $36,514 = 1.20×; $125,250 / $36,514 = 3.43×.
findings.suggested_fix: Update §15's asymmetry paragraph to match §1: "one year of heavy Sonnet 5.5 use = $43,800 versus one 7B training run at the optimal token budget = $36,514 — training is now cheaper than a year of rented usage at this rung, and renting only wins decisively at StarCoder2's 3.5T token budget (~$7×)". Replace "Never for cost" with a claim the numbers support ("build for control and specialisation; on cost alone the comparison is close at R3-optimal and decisive for renting").

findings.target_section: §12 Cost scenarios (all three) vs implementation-plan.md §9.4
findings.claim: Scenario A total $1,142 ("a real trained model and a working harness"), Scenario B central $232,362, Scenario C central $1.22×10^8 — presented as the project's cost.
findings.why_wrong: None of the three scenarios includes any of the engineering labour, which the same project's implementation plan costs at 152.5 person-weeks (≈165.8 pw with contingency) over 39 calendar weeks with 4 engineers. implementation-plan.md §9.4 explicitly excludes model/GPU/data/eval cost from that figure and defers them to compute-feasibility.md §12 — but §12 does not add the labour back, so the two documents' costings never meet. At a fully-loaded $200,000/engineer-year, 4 engineers × 39/52 years = $600,000 of harness labour, which is 2.7× Scenario A's entire total ($232k vs Scenario B's $232,362) and 71% of Scenario B's central estimate on its own. The calendar is affected too: implementation-plan.md's 39-week (≈9.0 month) harness schedule is longer than Scenario B's claimed "~5 months calendar" total for the model track (68 days of compute plus ~2 months of data prep = ~4.2 months), so the harness alone exceeds the model track's entire calendar.
findings.evidence: implementation-plan.md §9.4 ("152.5 pw", "≈165.8 pw" with contingency, "40 weeks elapsed ... calendar figure is 39 weeks", and "What this estimate does not include. It is an *engineering* estimate for the harness only ... Those are costed separately in `compute-feasibility.md` §12"); compute-feasibility.md §12 (no labour line in any scenario). Recomputation: $200,000 × 4 × 39/52 = $600,000; $600,000/$232,362 = 2.58×; $600,000/$232,362 = 258% (i.e. 2.58×, exceeding Scenario B's whole budget); 39/4.345 = 8.98 months vs (68/30.4 + 2) = 4.24 months.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a "Engineering labour" line to each scenario (person-weeks × a stated loaded rate) with the total calendar stated as the max of the harness calendar and the model calendar, not the model calendar alone. If the plan intends the two documents to be read separately, say so explicitly in §12 and state the combined project total somewhere both documents reference.

findings.target_section: §9 Timeline realism (team-size assumption) vs implementation-plan.md §9.1 Assumption A1
findings.claim: "**Team size assumption [SPECULATIVE TARGET]:** 2 people, one of whom can write distributed training code. This is stated so the numbers can be judged against a concrete plan."
findings.why_wrong: The project has two incompatible team sizes and the iteration-count arithmetic depends on which is right. compute-feasibility.md §9 assumes 2 people; implementation-plan.md §9.1 Assumption A1 states "The team is **4 engineers** for the duration"; llm-development-roadmap.md §14 uses four people; and compute-feasibility.md §12 Scenario C assumes "30–60 ML engineers × 2 years" for staff. The 2-person figure is not simply conservative — it is the stated basis for "a team of 2 gets roughly 4 runs in a year" (FEAS-10), for the "2 people, one of whom can write distributed training code" constraint on the data-prep and engineering columns, and for the §14 risk register's schedule estimates. With 4 people, either the number of parallel experiments rises (breaking the 4-runs/year figure, or requiring 2 concurrent 8-GPU allocations at ~$44.64/hr) or the harness work (§14's own "debugging the agent harness, which is usually where the actual schedule risk lives") is unstaffed.
findings.evidence: compute-feasibility.md §9 ("Team size assumption ... 2 people") and §12 Scenario C staff row ("30–60 ML engineers × 2 years"); implementation-plan.md §9.1 A1 ("The team is 4 engineers"); llm-development-roadmap.md §14 ("With a team of four"). Recomputation: 8×A100 = $22.32/hr; 8×H100 = $31.92/hr; two concurrent 8-GPU A100 allocations = $44.64/hr = ~$32,140/month; 365 d/68.16 d = 5.36 runs per allocation per year, so 2 allocations = 10.7 runs/year if both are free to run continuously (which the 68-day duration makes impossible on a 365-day year without queueing).
findings.suggested_fix: State one team size for the model track and reconcile it with implementation-plan.md §9.1, or state explicitly that they differ (e.g. 4 total, of whom 2 are on the model track) and recompute the iteration counts and the concurrent-fleet cost for the model-track subset.

findings.target_section: §5.1 Dataset storage table vs the §5.1 rule
findings.claim: "**[ESTIMATE]** The practical rule: **the filtered, tokenised corpus is 20–40% the size of the raw crawled corpus**, after deduplication and quality filtering. Budget for both simultaneously during the pipeline phase."
findings.why_wrong: Every row of the same table's "Raw source code to crawl/filter (est.)" column violates the rule stated immediately below it. The tokenised/raw ratios are: R0 48%, R1 58%/60%, R2 60%/60%, R3 56%/56%, R4 60%/57%, R5 56%, R6 56.7% — all above the stated 20–40% band. This matters because the raw-crawl column is what drives the data-pipeline line item in §12 ("crawl ~1 TB" for R3, "crawl ~110 TB" for R6) and the storage totals in §5.4, which are computed as if the two columns were independent. The ratio is also inconsistent with the project's own data plan, which states a 65.4% token-retention rate (34.6% of raw tokens removed by deduplication) for a 1.478×10^12-token corpus — a different figure again, implying that a single 20–40% rule does not describe the actual pipeline.
findings.evidence: compute-feasibility.md §5.1 table vs the rule in the same section; training-data-plan.md §4.4 ("retention 65.4%, i.e. 34.6% of raw tokens removed by deduplication"). Recomputation: R1-ext 2400/4000 = 60.0%; R2-ext 1200/2000 = 60.0%; R3-ext 14000/25000 = 56.0%; R5 5600/10000 = 56.0%; R6 62400/110000 = 56.7%; R0 2.4/5 = 48.0%; R3-opt 560/1000 = 56.0%. All exceed the stated 40% ceiling.
findings.suggested_fix: Either restate the rule to match the table (e.g. "the tokenised corpus is typically 50–60% the size of the raw crawl, since filtering removes files rather than tokens") and reconcile with training-data-plan.md's 65.4% token retention, or revise the raw-crawl column so the table satisfies the rule it states.

findings.target_section: §1.2 compute ladder table (R0 row), §1.2 iteration-count derivation
findings.claim: | **R0** | 30M | 0.6B | 1.08×10¹⁷ | 0.01 d | 3 s | **$1** | ~365 | — and the ladder's "Cost (corrected)" column for every row is presented without saying which hardware it prices.
findings.why_wrong: The roadmap's own ladder table has drifted from the upstream it corrects. (a) The R0 wall-clocks do not reproduce: true 8×A100 is 1.80 min and true 8×H100 is 0.51 min, but the table prints "0.01 d" (= 14.4 min) and "3 s"; the upstream §3.4 now prints 1.8 min and 0.5 min. (b) The R2-extended H100 wall-clock prints "5.0 d" where the true value is 8.77 d (1,684 GPU-h / 8 / 24) — a 1.75× understatement — while the same row's A100 cell (31 d) and cost cell ($16,767) are correct, so the row mixes conventions. (c) The "Cost (corrected)" column is silent about its basis: every row is priced on A100 ($97 / $1,677 / $36,514 / $912,861 / $167,668 match the true A100 cost exactly), yet the table has an adjacent "Wall on 8×H100" column whose true costs are far lower ($39 / $672 / $14,636 / $365,897 / $67,206). A reader comparing the A100 wall-clock to the H100 wall-clock will assume the cost column applies to both. (d) The R6 row prints "860 d (4,096 GPUs)" in a column headed "Wall on 8×A100"; true 8×A100 is 440,430 d and 860 d corresponds to 4,096 A100s.
findings.evidence: llm-development-roadmap.md §1.2 table vs compute-feasibility.md §3.4 table (patched 2026-10-22). Recomputation: R0 8×A100 = 0.2404/8×60 = 1.80 min (roadmap 0.01 d = 14.4 min); R0 8×H100 = 0.5 min (roadmap 3 s); R2-ext 8×H100 = 1,684/8/24 = 8.77 d (roadmap 5.0 d); R6 true 8×A100 = 84,562,500/8/24 = 440,430 d and 4,096×A100 = 860 d (roadmap puts 860 d under an "8xA100" header). Cost-column provenance check: every row equals the true A100 cost to within 0.01%.
findings.suggested_fix: Rebuild the roadmap ladder table from the patched upstream §3.4 (or add a script that regenerates it), fix the R0 and R2-ext H100 wall-clocks, label the cost column "Cost (8×A100)" explicitly, and correct the R6 row's column placement or its fleet annotation.

findings.claim: "**[KNOWN FACT]** `compute-feasibility.md` §8.3: a full evaluation sweep costs **$51** self-evaluated versus **$125,250** via API — a **2,400× advantage**, which is the entire economic argument for training our own model." And: "**[KNOWN FACT]** The compute path's own arithmetic, as stated upstream: R2 at the optimal token budget costs **~$13,413** and takes **~3 days on 8×A100**; R3 costs **~$292,115** and **~68 days**; Scenario A (R3 at optimal, with ~2 months data prep) is **~$844k** and **~5 months calendar**."
findings.why_wrong: The roadmap's §0.4 section is one of the documents that diagnosed and corrected the fleet error, so quoting the pre-correction figures as [KNOWN FACT] from the now-patched upstream is doubly wrong: the figures are both stale and mis-tagged (they are the roadmap's own ESTIMATE, not an upstream fact). Concretely: R2 is now $1,677 (not $13,413 — an 8× overstatement), R3 is now $36,514 (not $292,115), Scenario B is now $232,362 (not $844k, ~3.6×), and the "$844k" figure does not appear in the patched upstream at all. The $51-vs-$125,250 "2,400× advantage" quote is also the upstream §8.3 claim that FEAS-01 and FEAS-02 show to be a 30× workload mismatch — the roadmap describes it as "the entire economic argument for training our own model", which is the single most load-bearing sentence in its Path-1/Path-2 comparison. The roadmap's own §1.2 table already carries the corrected values, so the document contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: llm-development-roadmap.md line 1024 and line 1312 vs llm-development-roadmap.md §1.2 table (corrected: R2 $1,677, R3 $36,514, R3-ext $912,861) and vs the patched compute-feasibility.md §3.4 / §12 Scenario B central $232,362. Recomputation: $13,413 vs true $1,677 (8.0×); $292,115 vs true $36,514 (8.0×); $844,000 vs $232,362 (3.63×).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace both quotes with the corrected upstream values and re-tag them [ESTIMATE] with the upstream section reference. For the §8.3 quote, use the corrected matched-workload figure (~20× at 15,000 runs, per FEAS-01) and state the workload explicitly, rather than repeating a 30×-mismatched ratio as the load-bearing economic argument.
